docs.title: Candidates
docs.text:
In plain words

A candidate is a dip that passed our first checks. It is not a planet. Each one gets an ID (SS-0001, SS-0002, ...) and, once it survives vetting, a nickname. It needs two keys before it goes anywhere: my analysis, and your own check.

docs.title: Claims register
docs.text:
In plain words

Ahmed, every fact the book relies on lives here once, with how sure we are and where it came from. Pages show a small label next to a fact; tap it and you land on its row here.

docs.title: How to read the labels
docs.text: The shape carries the meaning, not the colour. VERIFIED (solid outline) means we read the original source or measured it ourselves. LIKELY (dashed) means a summary or secondary source. UNVERIFIED (dotted) means memory or one weak source: test before relying on it.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Every technical word in the book, in plain words. Pages link here the first time they use a term.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text: A dip in a light curve that passed our first checks and might be a planet. Not a planet until professionals confirm it.

docs.title: Circumbinary planet
docs.text: A planet that orbits both stars of a pair. Its dips come at irregular times, which is why standard searches miss them. Our main quest.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text: How much of the star's light a dip blocks, as a fraction: depth = (planet radius ÷ star radius)². Usually given in % or ppm.

docs.title: Eclipsing binary
docs.text: Two stars orbiting each other, lined up so that one passes in front of the other. Makes deep, regular dips.

docs.title: Light curve
docs.text: A star's brightness measured again and again over time and drawn as a graph: time along the bottom, brightness up the side.

docs.title: ppm
docs.text: Parts per million. 1% = 10,000 ppm. Earth crossing the Sun blocks about 84 ppm.

docs.title: Radius
docs.text: Distance from the centre of a star or planet to its edge. We measure planets in Earth radii and stars in Sun radii (the Sun is about 109 Earths wide).

docs.title: Sector
docs.text: One TESS stretch of about 27 days looking at the same patch of sky.

docs.title: TESS
docs.text: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018. It photographs most of the sky, one sector at a time. All its data is free.

docs.title: Transit
docs.text: A planet passing in front of its star as seen from Earth, which makes a small dip in the light curve.

main quest · active

Main quest: planets around two stars

Planets orbiting two stars dip at irregular times, so NASA's regular clock-based search misses them. First campaign: G1, Kepler-field binaries that TESS has watched again.

docs.title: Credit and publishing
docs.text:
What this chapter answers: once we find something, how does it become a recognised discovery with your name on it?

In plain words

Ahmed, a dip doesn't become "ours" when we see it. It becomes ours when it's written up and published, and then shared with the TESS team. In 2026 the rules changed: the public candidate site now wants the write-up published first. This chapter is the sample page for the book's chapter layout.

You need first: L6 Two-key vetting (outline).

docs.title: The order of steps
docs.text:
1. Two keys: my analysis and your own check both pass.
  2. Write-up: a short note in RNAAS (free), or a full paper with a professional team.
  3. ExoFOP: only a published candidate can be uploaded, and uploading needs approval VERIFIED. This rule arrived on 19 August 2026, after a pause that started on 31 March VERIFIED.
  4. TESS team: they decide whether it becomes a TOI.

docs.title: Journals and AI
docs.text:
• MNRAS: AI can't be an author, and how we used it (including code and data processing) goes in the cover letter and in the paper VERIFIED. You can submit without a university VERIFIED.
  • A&A: AI can't be an author; help with language, coding and searching needs no disclosure if a person oversees it LIKELY.

docs.title: What this means for our hunt
docs.text: Plan the write-up as part of vetting, not after it. The first candidate's timeline is: two keys, RNAAS draft, publication, then ExoFOP.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Does citing published tools we use count as "a previously published method" for an RNAAS route? Only ExoFOP support can say.

Sources: see the claims register. Last reviewed 2026-10-19.

docs.title: L1 How big is the dip?
docs.text:
Level 1 of 6 · 20 min · Maths: fractions, percentages, ppm, squares

In plain words

When a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a small circle of light. How much light it blocks tells you how big the planet is compared with the star. By the end of this level, Ahmed, you'll be able to look at a dip and say "that's planet-sized" or "that's a whole star".

docs.title: Why this matters for you
docs.text: Most dips in your G1 binaries are the two stars eclipsing each other. The first thing you'll do with any new dip, for the rest of the project, is ask: is it deep enough to be a star? This level gives you that test.

docs.title: The one idea
docs.text:
The fraction of light blocked is the depth:

depth = (planet radius ÷ star radius)²

Radius means centre to edge. It's squared because what's blocked is an area, and area grows with the square of the size. Double the planet's size and the dip gets four times deeper.

docs.title: Your exercise (on real data)
docs.text:
Exercise

  • File: TOI-1338, sector 97, 2-minute light curve (data/wave-3/lk/).
  • Command: py -3.12 learn/ex-L1.py (I prepare it; it marks one deep dip and prints its depth).
  • Write in your journal: is that dip planet-sized or star-sized, and why?

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
1. A planet half as wide as its star. What depth?

(1/2)² = 1/4 = 25%. That's far too big for a planet; it's the size of a star. When a dip is that deep, think "eclipsing binary", not "planet".

2. You double the planet's size. What happens to the depth?

It goes up 4× (2² = 4).

3. Why do small red stars help us find small planets?

The star is smaller, so the same planet blocks a bigger fraction: the dip is deeper and easier to see.

Summary: depth = (planet ÷ star)². Tiny dips (ppm) can be planets; huge dips (tens of %) are stars.

When you're done, tell Claude: "L1 done, n/3". Next: L2 turns a depth back into a size.
